note:
The Phoenician noun supports the two consonants. The database files the noun under אוה, whose desire words are in taavah. Egyptian jw, “island” (TLA 21940), also resembles it, but a direction of borrowing is uncertain.

Merged from `i-coastland`, `ay-where` on 2026-11-20: one root, one entry.
summary:
Tyre trades by sea with the coastlands. The kings of Tarshish and the islands bring tribute to the king in Psalm 72. The same consonants also spell the question word אֵי, “where?”, with which Yahweh asks Cain about Abel’s whereabouts.

The question asks someone’s location. In Genesis 3:9 God addresses the man directly. In Genesis 4:9 he asks Cain where Abel is.

senses.definition: Land approached by sea, also its inhabitants. Ezekiel describes the islands in the sea trembling at Tyre’s fall. Isaiah calls on the distant coastlands to listen.

evidence.note: אִיֵּי הַגּוֹיִם, “the coastlands of the nations,” names the inhabitants by their lands. They spread out, each according to his language.

senses.definition: Introduces a question asking where someone or something is.

evidence.note: Yahweh asks אֵי הֶבֶל אָחִיךָ, “Where is Abel your brother?” Cain answers that he does not know.

words.summary: This particle asks about location. Its historical relationship to the noun אִי is unclear.

senses.definition: Ask the location of a person identified by name or by a pronominal suffix.

evidence.note: God calls to the man. The suffix in אַיֶּכָּה identifies him as the person being asked, “Where are you?”
In אֵי הֶבֶל אָחִיךָ, “Where is Abel your brother?”, the name follows the interrogative.
